claim: The SARS-CoV-2 spike (S) protein is responsible for viral fusion with the host cell, initiating an infection that leads to COVID-19.
source: The SARS-CoV-2 spike (S) glycoprotein is responsible for viral fusion with the host cell, initiating an infection that leads to COVID-19 (Walls et al., 2020; Wrapp et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Walls et al., 2020 and Wrapp et al., 2020

claim: S is a homotrimer with a structure subdivided into two topological domains, namely S1 and S2, separated by a furin site.
source: S is a homotrimer with a structure subdivided into two topological domains, namely S1 and S2, see Figure 1a, separated by a furin site, which is cleaved in the pre-fusion architecture (Walls et al., 2020; Wrapp et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Walls et al., 2020 and Wrapp et al., 2020, and reference to Figure 1a

claim: The furin site is cleaved in the pre-fusion architecture.
source: S is a homotrimer with a structure subdivided into two topological domains, namely S1 and S2, see Figure 1a, separated by a furin site, which is cleaved in the pre-fusion architecture (Walls et al., 2020; Wrapp et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Walls et al., 2020 and Wrapp et al., 2020

claim: Host cell fusion is predominantly triggered by S binding to the angiotensin-converting Enzyme 2 (ACE2) receptor located on the host cell surface in WHu-1 and most variants of concern.
source: In the Wuhan-Hu-1 strain (WHu-1), and still in most variants of concern (VoCs), host cell fusion is predominantly triggered by S binding to the angiotensin-converting Enzyme 2 (ACE2) receptor located on the host cell surface (Jackson et al., 2022; Wrapp et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Jackson et al., 2022 and Wrapp et al., 2020

claim: S binding to ACE2 is supported by glycan co-receptors, such as heparan sulfate in the extracellular matrix.
source: This process is supported by glycan co-receptors, such as heparan sulfate (HS) in the extracellular matrix (Clausen et al., 2020; Kearns et al., 2022)
evidence: Supported by citations to Clausen et al., 2020 and Kearns et al., 2022

claim: S binding to ACE2 is supported by monosialylated gangliosides oligosaccharides (GM1os and GM2os) peeking from the surface of the host cells.
source: This process is supported by glycan co-receptors, such as heparan sulfate (HS) in the extracellular matrix (Clausen et al., 2020; Kearns et al., 2022) and by monosialylated gangliosides oligosaccharides (GM1os and GM2os) peeking from the surface of the host cells (Nguyen et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Nguyen et al., 2022

claim: The interaction with ACE2 requires a dramatic conformational change of the S, known as 'opening,' where one or more receptor binding domains (RBDs) in the S1 subdomain become exposed.
source: The interaction with ACE2 requires a dramatic conformational change of the S, known as 'opening,' where one or more receptor binding domains (RBDs) in the S1 subdomain become exposed.
evidence: This is established knowledge about SARS-CoV-2 spike protein mechanism

claim: The region of the RBD in direct contact with the ACE2 surface is known as receptor binding motif (RBM).
source: The region of the RBD in direct contact with the ACE2 surface is known as receptor binding motif (RBM) (Jackson et al., 2022; Lan et al., 2020; Yi et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Jackson et al., 2022, Lan et al., 2020, and Yi et al., 2020

claim: S binding to ACE2 causes shedding of the S1 subdomain and the transition to a post-fusion conformation, which exposes the fusion peptide near the host cell surface, leading to viral entry.
source: Ultimately, S binding to ACE2 causes shedding of the S1 subdomain and the transition to a post-fusion conformation, which exposes the fusion peptide near the host cell surface, leading to viral entry (Dodero-Rojas et al., 2021; Jackson et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dodero-Rojas et al., 2021 and Jackson et al., 2022

claim: Enveloped viruses hijack the host cell's glycosylation machinery to cover S with a dense coat of host carbohydrates, known as a glycan shield.
source: To evade the host immune system, enveloped viruses hijack the host cell's glycosylation machinery to cover S with a dense coat of host carbohydrates, known as a glycan shield (Casalino et al., 2020; Chawla et al., 2022; Grant et al., 2020; Turoňová et al., 2020; Watanabe et al., 2020b; Watanabe et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations including Casalino et al., 2020, Chawla et al., 2022, Grant et al., 2020, Turoňová et al., 2020, Watanabe et al., 2020b, and Watanabe et al., 2019

claim: In SARS-CoV-2 the glycan shield screens effectively over 60% of the S protein surface.
source: In SARS-CoV-2 the glycan shield screens effectively over 60% of the S protein surface (Casalino et al., 2020)
evidence: Supported by citation to Casalino et al., 2020

claim: The RBD is targeted by approximately 90% of serum neutralising antibodies.
source: The RBD targeted by approximately 90% of serum neutralising antibodies (Piccoli et al., 2020)
evidence: Supported by citation to Piccoli et al., 2020

claim: The SARS-CoV-2 S RBD from the WHu-1 to the EG.5.1 shows two highly conserved N-glycosylation sites, one at N331 and the other at N343.
source: The SARS-CoV-2 S RBD (aa 327–540) from the WHu-1 (China, 2019) to the EG.5.1 (China, 2023) shows two highly conserved N-glycosylation sites (Harbison et al., 2022), one at N331 and the other at N343 (Watanabe et al., 2020a).
evidence: Supported by citations to Harbison et al., 2022 and Watanabe et al., 2020a

claim: Glycosylation at N331 is located on a highly flexible region linking the RBD to the NTD.
source: While glycosylation at N331 is located on a highly flexible region linking the RBD to the NTD, the N343 glycan covers a large portion of the RBD (Casalino et al., 2020; Harbison et al., 2022)
evidence: Supported by citations to Casalino et al., 2020 and Harbison et al., 2022

claim: The N343 glycan covers a large portion of the RBD, stretching across the protein surface and forming a bridge connecting the two helical regions that frame the beta-sheet core.
source: While glycosylation at N331 is located on a highly flexible region linking the RBD to the NTD, the N343 glycan covers a large portion of the RBD (Casalino et al., 2020; Harbison et al., 2022), stretching across the protein surface and forming a bridge connecting the two helical regions that frame the beta-sheet core, see Figure 1b.
evidence: Supported by citations to Casalino et al., 2020 and Harbison et al., 2022, and reference to Figure 1b

claim: Removal of the N343 glycan induces a conformational change which in WHu-1, alpha, and beta allosterically controls the structure and dynamics of the RBM.
source: In this work, we show that removal of the N343 glycan induces a conformational change which in WHu-1, alpha, and beta allosterically controls the structure and dynamics of the RBM, see Figure 1c.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1c from MD simulations

claim: In delta and omicron, the effects of N343 glycan removal on RBM structure and dynamics are significantly dampened by mutations that strengthen the RBD architecture.
source: In delta and omicron these effects are significantly dampened by mutations that strengthen the RBD architecture.
evidence: Based on MD simulation results presented in the manuscript

claim: Enzymatic removal of the N343 glycan affects binding of monosialylated ganglioside co-receptors in the WHu-1 RBD, but not in delta.
source: Further to this molecular insight, we show that enzymatic removal of the N343 glycan affects binding of monosialylated ganglioside co-receptors (Nguyen et al., 2022) in the WHu-1 RBD, but not in delta.
evidence: Supported by experimental ESI-MS affinity measurements presented in the manuscript

claim: The affinity of the RBD for GM1os and GM2os changes significantly across the VoCs, with beta and omicron exhibiting the weakest binding.
source: We also observe that the affinity of the RBD for GM1 GM1os and GM2 GM1os changes significantly across the VoCs, with beta and omicron exhibiting the weakest binding.
evidence: Supported by experimental ESI-MS affinity measurements presented in the manuscript

claim: The structured region of the RBD is supported by a largely hydrophobic beta sheet core, framed by two flanking, partially helical loops (aa 335–345 and aa 365–375), linked by a bridging N-glycan at N343.
source: The structured region is supported by a largely hydrophobic beta sheet core, framed by two flanking, partially helical loops (aa 335–345 and aa 365–375), linked by a bridging N-glycan at N343, see Figure 1b.
evidence: Supported by structural analysis from MD simulations and reference to Figure 1b

claim: The aa 335–345 loop carries the N343 glycosylation site and it is part of an important antigenic region targeted by Class 2 and 3 antibodies.
source: The aa 335–345 loop carries the N343 glycosylation site and it is part of an important antigenic region targeted by Class 2 and 3 antibodies (Bangaru et al., 2022; Barnes et al., 2020; Carabelli et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bangaru et al., 2022, Barnes et al., 2020, Carabelli et al., 2023, and Chen et al., 2023

claim: In the bridging conformation, the N343 glycan pentasaccharide extends across the RBD beta sheet to reach the aa 365–375 loop forming highly populated hydrogen bonding and dispersion interactions with the backbone and with the sidechains of residues 365–375.
source: In the bridging conformation, the N343 glycan pentasaccharide extends across the RBD beta sheet to reach the aa 365–375 loop forming highly populated hydrogen bonding and dispersion interactions with the backbone and with the sidechains of residues 365–375, see Figure 1b,c and Appendix 1—figure 2.
evidence: Supported by MD simulation data shown in Figure 1b,c and Appendix 1—figure 2

claim: The bridging N343 glycan shields the hydrophobic beta sheet core of the RBD from the surrounding water, preventing energetically unfavourable contacts.
source: The bridging N343 glycan shields the hydrophobic beta sheet core of the RBD from the surrounding water, preventing energetically unfavourable contacts.
evidence: Based on MD simulation observations and structural analysis

claim: The N343 glycan forms dispersion interactions with the hydrophobic residues of the beta sheet through its core GlcNAc-β(1-4)GlcNAc, while engaging in hydrogen bonds with the surrounding water and with the aa 365–375 helical loop.
source: Due to its amphipathic nature, the N343 forms dispersion interactions with the hydrophobic residues of the beta sheet through its core GlcNAc-β(1-4)GlcNAc, while engaging in hydrogen bonds with the surrounding water and with the aa 365–375 helical loop.
evidence: Based on MD simulation observations of molecular interactions

claim: The key anchoring residues S371, S373, and S375 within the aa 365–375 loop are all mutated to hydrophobic residues in all omicron variants (BA.1–2, BA.4–5, BQ.1.1, EG.5.1, XBB.1.5).
source: Notably, the key anchoring residues S371, S373, and S375 within this loop are all mutated to hydrophobic residues in all omicron variants (BA.1–2, BA.4–5, BQ.1.1, EG.5.1, XBB.1.5).
evidence: Based on sequence analysis of omicron variants

claim: The RBM encompasses aa 439–506 and counts all the RBD residues in direct contact with ACE2.
source: The RBM encompasses aa 439–506 and counts all the RBD residues in direct contact with ACE2 (Lan et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lan et al., 2020

claim: The RBM is heavily targeted by both Class 1 and 2 antibodies.
source: The RBM is heavily targeted by both Class 1 and 2 antibodies (Bangaru et al., 2022; Barnes et al., 2020; Carabelli et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2023)
evidence: Supported by citations to Bangaru et al., 2022, Barnes et al., 2020, Carabelli et al., 2023, and Chen et al., 2023

claim: All VoCs carry mutations in the RBM region.
source: The RBM is heavily targeted by both Class 1 and 2 antibodies (Bangaru et al., 2022; Barnes et al., 2020; Carabelli et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2023) and under high evolutionary pressure, with all VoCs carrying mutations in this region.
evidence: Based on sequence analysis of variants of concern

claim: The RBM in unbound S is largely unstructured and dynamic.
source: As shown by earlier MD simulations studies (Casalino et al., 2020; Harbison et al., 2022; Sztain et al., 2021; Williams et al., 2022), the RBM in unbound S is largely unstructured and dynamic, an insight also supported by the low resolution cryo-EM maps of this region (Gobeil et al., 2022; Walls et al., 2020; Wrapp et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to MD simulation studies and cryo-EM structural data

claim: The RBM's inherent flexibility is likely an important feature in the opening and closing mechanism of the RBD.
source: The RBM's inherent flexibility is likely an important feature in the opening and closing mechanism of the RBD, where the N343 from adjacent RBDs engage with the protein in closed conformation and gate RBD opening (Sztain et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sztain et al., 2021 and involves speculation about functional importance

claim: The N343 from adjacent RBDs engage with the protein in closed conformation and gate RBD opening.
source: The RBM's inherent flexibility is likely an important feature in the opening and closing mechanism of the RBD, where the N343 from adjacent RBDs engage with the protein in closed conformation and gate RBD opening (Sztain et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sztain et al., 2021

claim: The only relatively structured region of the RBM is the hydrophilic patch, a hairpin stabilised by a network of interlocking salt-bridges and polar residues, namely R454, R457, K458, K462, E465, D467, S469, and E471.
source: The only relatively structured region of the RBM is what we define here on as the hydrophilic patch, see Figure 1b and a hairpin stabilised by a network of interlocking salt-bridges and polar residues, namely R454, R457, K458, K462, E465, D467, S469, and E471, that faces the interior of the S when the RBD is closed.
evidence: Based on structural analysis from MD simulations and reference to Figure 1b

claim: When in complex with ACE2 or with antibodies, the RBM adopts a structured fold, also shared by the SARS-CoV-1 S RBD.
source: When in complex with ACE2 or with antibodies, the RBM adopts a structured fold, also shared by the SARS-CoV-1 S RBD (Li et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Li et al., 2005

claim: In the ACE2-bound conformation, only the terminal hairpin of the RBM (aa 476–486) retains a high degree of flexibility.
source: In this conformation, only the terminal hairpin of the RBM (aa 476–486) retains a high degree of flexibility, as shown in this work and by others (Williams et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by MD simulation data in this work and citation to Williams et al., 2022

claim: The RBM-bound fold is stabilised by a hydrophobic patch supported by the stacking of the aromatic and aliphatic residues L455, F456, Y473, A475.
source: The RBM-bound fold is stabilised by a hydrophobic patch supported by the stacking of the aromatic and aliphatic residues L455, F456, Y473, A475, see Figure 1b, which are part of the protein interface with ACE2.
evidence: Based on structural analysis from MD simulations and reference to Figure 1b

claim: All residues in the hydrophobic and hydrophilic patches are highly conserved across the VoCs, possibly due to their critical function in inducing and/or stabilising the RBD into its ACE2-bound conformation.
source: Notably, all residues in the hydrophobic and hydrophilic patches are highly conserved across the VoCs, possibly due to their critical function in inducing and/or stabilising the RBD into its ACE2-bound conformation.
evidence: Based on sequence analysis and involves speculation about functional importance

claim: The loss of stacking in the hydrophobic patch due to the recent F456L mutation in the EG.5.1 variant is recovered by the L455F mutation in the FLip variant.
source: As an interesting observation, the loss of stacking in the hydrophobic patch due to the recent F456L mutation in the EG.5.1 variant (China, 2023) is recovered by the L455F mutation in the, appropriately named, FLip variant.
evidence: Based on sequence analysis and structural inference

claim: Region 1 stretches from aa 337–353, which includes the N343 glycosylation site, and counts residues targeted by class 2 and 3 antibodies.
source: Region 1 stretches from aa 337–353, which includes the N343 glycosylation site, and counts residues targeted by class 2 and 3 antibodies (Bangaru et al., 2022; Carabelli et al., 2023; Harvey et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bangaru et al., 2022, Carabelli et al., 2023, and Harvey et al., 2021

claim: The aa sequence in Region 1 has been highly conserved so far, allowing specific antibodies to retain their neutralisation activity across all VoCs, such as S309.
source: The aa sequence in Region 1 has been highly conserved so far, allowing specific antibodies to retain their neutralisation activity across all VoCs, such as S309 (Newby et al., 2023; Watanabe et al., 2020a), whose binding mode also directly involves the N343 glycan (Liu et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Newby et al., 2023, Watanabe et al., 2020a, and Liu et al., 2021

claim: The S309 antibody binding mode directly involves the N343 glycan.
source: The aa sequence in Region 1 has been highly conserved so far, allowing specific antibodies to retain their neutralisation activity across all VoCs, such as S309 (Newby et al., 2023; Watanabe et al., 2020a), whose binding mode also directly involves the N343 glycan (Liu et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Liu et al., 2021

claim: The BA.2.86 variant carries the K356T mutation which introduces a new N-glycosylation sequon at N354.
source: A notable and dramatic exception to this high degree of conservation in Region 1 is given by the BA.2.86 variant (Denmark, 2023), known as 'pirola,' where the K356T mutation introduces a new N-glycosylation sequon at N354.
evidence: Based on sequence analysis of BA.2.86 variant

claim: Region 2 coincides with the RBM.
source: Region 2 coincides with the RBM, which, in addition to binding ACE2 and neutralising antibodies, used to bind the N370 glycan from adjacent RBDs (Allen et al., 2023; Harbison et al., 2022; Watanabe et al., 2020b).
evidence: This is a definition provided by the authors

claim: The RBM used to bind the N370 glycan from adjacent RBDs.
source: Region 2 coincides with the RBM, which, in addition to binding ACE2 and neutralising antibodies, used to bind the N370 glycan from adjacent RBDs (Allen et al., 2023; Harbison et al., 2022; Watanabe et al., 2020b).
evidence: Supported by citations to Allen et al., 2023, Harbison et al., 2022, and Watanabe et al., 2020b

claim: N370 glycosylation is lost in SARS-CoV-2 S with the RBM binding cleft available to bind glycan co-receptors.
source: N370 glycosylation is lost in SARS-CoV-2 S with the RBM binding cleft available to bind glycan co-receptors, such as glycosaminoglycans (Clausen et al., 2020; Kearns et al., 2022), blood group antigens (Nguyen et al., 2022; Wu et al., 2023), monosialylated gangliosides (Nguyen et al., 2022), among others.
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies on glycan co-receptor binding

claim: Region 3 is a short, relatively structured loop stretching between aa 411–426, located on the opposite side of the RBD relative to Region 1.
source: Region 3 is a short, relatively structured loop stretching between aa 411–426, located on the opposite side of the RBD relative to Region 1, see Figure 1d.
evidence: Based on structural analysis and reference to Figure 1d

claim: Extensive sampling through conventional MD and GaMD shows that the loss of N343 glycosylation induces a dramatic conformational change in the WHu-1, alpha, and beta RBDs, where one or both helical loops flanking the hydrophobic beta sheet core pull towards each other.
source: Extensive sampling through conventional MD, i.e., 4 μs for the alpha and beta VoC and 8 μs with an additional 4 μs of Gaussian accelerated MD (GaMD) for the WHu-1 RBD, see Appendix 1—table 1, shows that the loss of N343 glycosylation induces a dramatic conformational change in the RBD, where one or both helical loops flanking the hydrophobic beta sheet core pull towards each other, see Figure 2.
evidence: Supported by MD simulation data shown in Figure 2 and Appendix 1—table 1

claim: The conformational change upon loss of N343 glycosylation can occur very rapidly or after a longer delay due to the complexity of the conformational energy landscape.
source: This conformational change can occur very rapidly upon removal of the N-glycan or after a longer delay due to the complexity of the conformational energy landscape.
evidence: Based on observations from MD simulations

claim: In the WHu-1 RBD, the structure of Region 1 is stable, largely due to the contribution of the bridging N343 glycan forming hydrogen bonds with the residues in loop aa 365–375 throughout the simulations.
source: As shown by the RMSD values distributions, represented through Kernel Density Estimates (KDE) in Figure 2, the structure of Region 1 in the WHu-1 RBD is stable. In the glycosylated RBD, the stability of Region 1 is largely due to the contribution of the bridging N343 glycan, chosen here to be a complex biantennary FA2G2 form based on Watanabe et al., 2020a, forming hydrogen bonds with the residues in loop aa 365–375 throughout the simulations, see Figure 1c and Appendix 1—figure 2.
evidence: Supported by MD simulation data shown in Figure 2, Figure 1c, and Appendix 1—figure 2

claim: The conformation of the RBM (Region 2) is very flexible in both glycosylated and non-glycosylated WHu-1 RBD forms.
source: Conversely, the conformation of the RBM (Region 2) is very flexible in both glycosylated and non-glycosylated forms.
evidence: Based on MD simulation observations

claim: Loss of N343 glycosylation triggers a conformational change in Region 1 of the WHu-1 RBD that ultimately triggers the complete detachment of the hydrophilic loop from Region 1 through rupture of the non-covalent interactions network between Y351 and S469 or T470 and between Y351 and L452.
source: Loss of N343 glycosylation triggers a conformational change in the Region 1 of the WHu-1 RBD, shown by a broader KDE peak in Figure 2a. This conformational change ultimately triggers the complete detachment of the hydrophilic loop from Region 1, see Figure 1c, through rupture of the non-covalent interactions network between Y351 (Region 1) and S469 or T470 (Region 2) via of hydrogen bonding, and Y351 and L452 (Region 2) via CH-π stacking.
evidence: Supported by MD simulation data shown in Figure 2a and Figure 1c

claim: Structural changes in Region 3 upon loss of glycosylation at N343 appear to be negligible in WHu-1.
source: Structural changes in Region 3 upon loss of glycosylation at N343 appear to be negligible.
evidence: Based on MD simulation observations

claim: In the alpha RBD, the loss of glycosylation at N343 causes a swift conformational change that brings the aa 335–345 and aa 365–375 loops closer together.
source: Again, we see that the loss of glycosylation at N343 causes a swift conformational change that brings the aa 335–345 and aa 365–375 loops closer together, see Figure 2b.
evidence: Supported by MD simulation data shown in Figure 2b

claim: In the alpha RBD, the conformational change upon loss of N343 glycosylation involves primarily Region 1 and ultimately determines the detachment of the hydrophilic patch from the Y351 in Region 1.
source: This conformational change involves primarily Region 1, and just like the previous case, it ultimately determines the detachment of the hydrophilic patch from the Y351 in Region 1.
evidence: Based on MD simulation observations

claim: In the N343 glycosylated alpha RBD, a small conformational change in Region 3 involves a partial disruption and refolding of a helical turn.
source: Also shown by the KDE plot in Figure 2b and a small conformational change in Region 3, which involves a partial disruption and refolding of a helical turn, can be observed during the trajectory of the N343 glycosylated alpha RBD.
evidence: Supported by MD simulation data shown in Figure 2b

claim: In the beta RBD, the reconstructed N343 glycan adopts a bridging conformation quite rapidly and retains this conformation throughout the trajectory with only minor deviations.
source: In the beta RBD (starting structure from PDB 7LYN) the reconstructed N343 glycan adopts a bridging conformation quite rapidly and retains this conformation throughout the trajectory with only minor deviations.
evidence: Based on MD simulation observations

claim: In the beta RBD, loss of glycosylation at N343 causes a rapid tightening of the RBD core helical loops towards each other, which ultimately causes the detachment of the hydrophilic loop from Y351 in Region 1 towards the end of the MD trajectory.
source: Loss of glycosylation at N343 causes a rapid tightening of the RBD core helical loops towards each other, which again in this case ultimately causes the detachment of the hydrophilic loop from Y351 in Region 1 towards the end of the MD trajectory, i.e., after 1.9 μs of sampling.
evidence: Based on MD simulation observations

claim: The WHu-1 RBD binds monosialylated gangliosides as co-receptors in SARS-CoV-2 infection.
source: Earlier work from some of us shows that the WHu-1 RBD binds monosialylated gangliosides as co-receptors in SARS-CoV-2 infection (Nguyen et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Nguyen et al., 2022

claim: The predicted GM1os binding site is located at the junction between Region 1 and Region 2 of the WHu-1 RBD and it involves all the residues that stabilise the region, namely Y351, L452, S469, and T470.
source: The predicted GM1os binding site is located at the junction between Region 1 and Region 2 of the WHu-1 RBD and it involves all the residues that stabilise the region, namely Y351, L452, S469, and T470, see Figures 1c and 2e.
evidence: Based on MD simulation predictions shown in Figures 1c and 2e

claim: EndoF3-treatment trims down the fucosylated biantennary and triantennary complex N-glycans into core nonfucosylated or fucosylated GlcNAc (Gn or GnF, respectively).
source: Here, we used endoF3-treatment to trim down the fucosylated biantennary and triantennary complex N-glycans into core nonfucosylated or fucosylated GlcNAc (Gn or GnF, respectively).
evidence: This is established knowledge about endoF3 enzyme activity

claim: LC-MS analysis suggests that N-glycans on N343 but not N331 of WHu-1 RBD were trimmed down by endoF3 treatment.
source: LC-MS analysis suggests that N-glycans on N343 but not N331 of WHu-1 RBD were trimmed down (Appendix 1—figure 6).
evidence: Supported by LC-MS data shown in Appendix 1—figure 6

claim: 31% of detected glycoforms in endoF3-treated WHu-1 RBD contained Gn/GnF at N343, while the remaining was the intact form.
source: From the zero-charge mass spectra of endoF3-treated WT RBD (Appendix 1—figure 5), we performed glycan assignment (Appendix 1—table 8) and found that 31% of detected glycoforms contained Gn/GnF at N343, while the remaining was the intact form.
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Appendix 1—figure 5 and Appendix 1—table 8

claim: Enzymatic removal of the N343 glycan from the WHu-1 RBD causes a complete loss of GM1os/2os binding.
source: Affinity data in Figure 2d show that the enzymatic removal of the N343 glycan from the WHu-1 RBD causes a complete loss of GM1os/2os binding, which is consistent with both, the involvement of the junction between Regions 1 and 2 the binding and its allosteric control of the RBM dynamics.
evidence: Supported by ESI-MS affinity data shown in Figure 2d

claim: Binding of GM1os and GM2os to the alpha RBD appears to be slightly decreased relative to WHu-1.
source: Furthermore, while binding of GM1os and GM2os to the alpha RBD appears to be slightly decreased relative to WHu-1, binding to the beta RBD is dramatically reduced.
evidence: Based on ESI-MS affinity measurements

claim: Binding of GM1os and GM2os to the beta RBD is dramatically reduced relative to WHu-1.
source: Furthermore, while binding of GM1os and GM2os to the alpha RBD appears to be slightly decreased relative to WHu-1, binding to the beta RBD is dramatically reduced.
evidence: Based on ESI-MS affinity measurements

claim: The E484K mutation in beta changes the key interaction between E484 and GM1os.
source: We can reconcile this finding with the mutation E484K in beta, which changes the key interaction between E484 and GM1os, see Figure 2
evidence: Based on structural analysis and inference from the predicted binding site

claim: Changes in structure and dynamics of the RBM terminal hairpin induced by mutations have been suggested to affect the S opening kinetics.
source: We can reconcile this finding with the mutation E484K in beta, which changes the key interaction between E484 and GM1os, see Figure 2 and with changes in structure and dynamics of the RBM terminal hairpin induced by mutations (Williams et al., 2022), which have also been suggested to affect the S opening kinetics (Wang et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Williams et al., 2022 and Wang et al., 2021

claim: The delta RBD carries two mutations, namely L452R and T478K, relative to the WHu-1 strain.
source: The delta (B.1.617.2) RBD carries two mutations, namely L452R and T478K, relative to the WHu-1 strain.
evidence: Based on sequence analysis of delta variant

claim: In the glycosylated delta RBD, the N343 glycan is observed to be much more dynamic than in the WHu-1, alpha, and beta RBDs, engaging in contacts with different regions of the RBD in addition to the loop aa 365–375.
source: In the glycosylated delta RBD the N343 glycan is observed to be much more dynamic than in the WHu-1, alpha, and beta RBDs, engaging in contacts with different regions of the RBD in addition to the loop aa 365–375.
evidence: Based on MD simulation observations

claim: In the delta RBD, the RBM (Region 2) is highly dynamic, with flexibility appearing to involve specifically the terminal hairpin of the RBM (aa 476–486), which includes the T478K mutation.
source: All trajectories, and in particular the results of the GaMD simulation in Figure 3c, show that RBM (Region 2) of delta is highly dynamic. This flexibility appears to involve specifically the terminal hairpin of the RBM (aa 476–486), which includes the T478K mutation, while the rest of the RBM is tightly anchored due to the L454R mutation.
evidence: Supported by MD simulation data shown in Figure 3c

claim: In the delta RBD, the R452 can establish a new hydrogen bond with Y351, in addition to S469 and T470, reinforcing the junction between Regions 1 and 2.
source: More specifically, the R452 of delta can establish a new hydrogen bond with Y351, in addition to S469 and T470, reinforcing the junction between Regions 1 and 2.
evidence: Based on MD simulation observations

claim: In the delta RBM, the role of L452 in CH-π stacking to Y351 is taken by the proximal L492, through a twist of the beta sheet.
source: Furthermore, in the delta RBM the role of L452 in CH-π stacking to Y351 is taken by the proximal L492, through a twist of the beta sheet, see Figure 3e.
evidence: Supported by MD simulation data shown in Figure 3e

claim: In the delta RBD, the tightening of the helical loops occurring upon loss of glycosylation at N343 does not affect the structure and dynamic of the junction between Regions 1 and 2.
source: As a consequence of the L452R mutation shown in Figure 3, the tightening of the helical loops aa 335–345 and aa 365–375 over the hydrophobic core of the RBD occurring upon loss of glycosylation at N343 does not affect the structure and dynamic of the junction between Regions 1 and 2, see Appendix 1—figure 3.
evidence: Supported by MD simulation data shown in Figure 3 and Appendix 1—figure 3

claim: In the delta RBD, the tightening of the loops upon loss of N343 glycosylation is mainly achieved by a larger displacement of the aa 365–375 loop rather than of Region 1 in conventional MD simulations.
source: Results of the conventional MD simulation show that the tightening of the loops is mainly achieved by a larger displacement of the aa 365–375 loop rather than of Region 1, while the GaMD results show tightening of both loops, see Appendix 1—figure 3.
evidence: Supported by MD simulation data shown in Appendix 1—figure 3

claim: In the delta RBD, the structure of the junction between Regions 1 and 2 remains undisturbed upon loss of N343 glycosylation, with no detachment of the hydrophilic patch within the sampling collected.
source: In all simulations, the structure of the junction between Regions 1 and 2 remains undisturbed, with no detachment of the hydrophilic patch within the sampling we collected.
evidence: Based on MD simulation observations

claim: Both N331 and N343 glycans in the delta RBD were trimmed down to Gn/GnF by endoF3 treatment.
source: From the zero-charge mass spectra of endoF3-treated RBD, see Appendix 1—figure 5, we performed glycan assignment, see Appendix 1—table 9, and found that both N331 and N343 glycans were trimmed down to Gn/GnF.
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Appendix 1—figure 5 and Appendix 1—table 9

claim: The delta RBD shows no loss of GM1os/2os binding upon loss of N343 glycosylation.
source: Direct ESI-MS data in Figure 3f show no loss of GM1/2 binding in the delta RBD upon loss of N343 glycosylation, which further supports the involvement of the Region 1–2 junction in sialylated glycans recognition.
evidence: Supported by ESI-MS affinity data shown in Figure 3f

claim: The omicron BA.1 RBD carries 15 mutations relative to the WHu-1 strain, namely S371L, S373P, S375F, K417N, N440K, G446S, S477N, T478K, E484A, Q493R, G496S, Q498R, N501Y, Y505H, and T547K.
source: The omicron BA.1 RBD carries 15 mutations relative to the WHu-1 strain, namely S371L, S373P, S375F, K417N, N440K, G446S, S477N, T478K, E484A, Q493R, G496S, Q498R, N501Y, Y505H, and T547K.
evidence: Based on sequence analysis of omicron BA.1 variant

claim: The S371L, S373P, and S375F mutations are retained in all omicron VoCs including the most recently circulating XBB.1.5, EG.5.1, and BA.2.86.
source: The S371L, S373P, and S375F mutations, retained in all omicron VoCs including the most recently circulating XBB.1.5, EG.5.1, and BA.2.86, remove all hydroxyl sidechains that we have seen being involved in hydrogen bonding interactions with the N343 glycan in the WHu-1, alpha, beta, and delta RBDs, see Figure 1c and Appendix 1—figure 3.
evidence: Based on sequence analysis and MD simulation data shown in Figure 1c and Appendix 1—figure 3

claim: The S371L, S373P, and S375F mutations remove all hydroxyl sidechains that were involved in hydrogen bonding interactions with the N343 glycan in the WHu-1, alpha, beta, and delta RBDs.
source: The S371L, S373P, and S375F mutations, retained in all omicron VoCs including the most recently circulating XBB.1.5, EG.5.1, and BA.2.86, remove all hydroxyl sidechains that we have seen being involved in hydrogen bonding interactions with the N343 glycan in the WHu-1, alpha, beta, and delta RBDs, see Figure 1c and Appendix 1—figure 3.
evidence: Based on MD simulation data shown in Figure 1c and Appendix 1—figure 3

claim: Despite the S371L, S373P, and S375F mutations in omicron BA.1, the N343 glycan still forms stable contacts with the aa 365–375 loop.
source: The results of the MD1 and GaMD simulations show that, despite the S371L, S373P, and S375F mutations, the N343 glycan is still forms stable contacts with the aa 365–375 loop, see Figure 1c and Appendix 1—figure 3, and these interactions contribute to the stability of the RBD structure, see Figure 4.
evidence: Supported by MD simulation data shown in Figure 1c, Appendix 1—figure 3, and Figure 4

claim: In all omicron BA.1 simulations, the loss of glycosylation at N343 causes a tightening of the aa 335–345 and aa 365–375 loops, which is stabilised by more efficient packing of the aa 365–375 loop within the hydrophobic core, driven by the embedding of the L371 and F375 sidechains.
source: In all simulations, the loss of glycosylation at N343 causes a tightening of the aa 335–345 and aa 365–375 loops, which in omicron is stabilised by more efficient packing of the aa 365–375 loop within the hydrophobic core, driven by the embedding of the L371 and F375 sidechains.
evidence: Based on MD simulation observations

claim: In the non-glycosylated omicron BA.1 RBD, there is no detachment of the hydrophilic patch.
source: The non-glycosylated RBD adopts a stable conformation where we do not see a detachment of the hydrophilic patch.
evidence: Based on MD simulation observations

claim: Omicron (BA.1) binds GM1os/2os only weakly.
source: The stabilising effect of the aa 365–375 loop mutations in omicron could not be tested by means of affinity for GM1os/2os as omicron (BA.1) binds those epitopes only weakly, see Figure 3f.
evidence: Supported by ESI-MS affinity data shown in Figure 3f

claim: The loss of E484 due to the E484A mutation in omicron may negate GM1os/2os binding.
source: Based on the binding site we predicted by MD simulations, see Figures 1d and 2e, and as observed for beta, the loss of E484 due to the E484A mutation in omicron may negate GM1os/2os binding.
evidence: Based on inference from the predicted binding site structure and comparison with beta

claim: The presence of an additional N-glycosylation site at N354 in BA.2.86 changes the conformation of the loop that hosts the site relative to the BA.1 structure.
source: The presence of an additional N-glycosylation site at N354 also changes the conformation of the loop that hosts the site relative to the BA.1 starting structure we used as a template to run the MD simulation, see Figure 4f.
evidence: Supported by MD simulation data shown in Figure 4f

claim: In BA.2.86, the N-glycans at N343 and N354 are tightly intertwined throughout the trajectory stabilising Region 1.
source: As shown in Figure 4d–f, the N-glycans at N343 and N354 are tightly intertwined throughout the trajectory stabilising Region 1, also shielding the area very effectively.
evidence: Supported by MD simulation data shown in Figure 4d–f

claim: The RBD has evolved since the WHu-1, alpha, and beta strains to make the N-glycosylation site at N343 structurally dispensable.
source: Taken together, our results show that since the WHu-1, alpha, and beta strains, the RBD has evolved to make the N-glycosylation site at N343 structurally dispensable.
evidence: Based on inference from the cumulative MD simulation results across variants

claim: A shift of the N343 glycosylation site within the sequence can potentially occur, provided that an N-glycosylation site in the immediate vicinity of N343 is necessary for folding and for function.
source: Within this framework, provided that an N-glycosylation site in the immediate vicinity of N343 is necessary for folding and for function, a shift of the site within the sequence can potentially occur.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the structural findings

claim: A shift of the N343 glycosylation site may negatively affect recognition and binding by neutralising antibodies and thus promote evasion.
source: Such a modification may negatively affect recognition and binding by neutralising antibodies (Liu et al., 2021; Piccoli et al., 2020; Pinto et al., 2020) and thus promote evasion.
evidence: Supported by citations and involves speculation about evolutionary consequences

claim: The new glycosylation site at N354 in BA.2.86 can effectively contribute to the stability of Region 1, while significantly increasing shielding.
source: We have also shown for the BA.2.86 that the new glycosylation site at N354 can effectively contribute to the stability of Region 1, while significantly increasing shielding.
evidence: Based on MD simulation results for BA.2.86

claim: Specific VoCs lost affinity for monosialylated ganglioside oligosaccharides with a trend in agreement with a binding site located at the junction between Region 1 and the RBM.
source: Moreover, we show that specific VoCs lost affinity for monosialylated ganglioside oligosaccharides with a trend in agreement with a binding site located at the junction between Region 1 and the RBM, which is part of the N370 glycan binding cleft on the RBD (Harbison et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by ESI-MS affinity data and citation to Harbison et al., 2022

claim: Further mutations may switch the affinity for monosialylated ganglioside oligosaccharides back on or determine a shift of preference of the RBD towards other glycans that can still be recognised within the N370 cleft.
source: Further to this, as mutations we identified dampened binding to monosialylated ganglioside oligosaccharides, it is also possible that further mutations may switch the affinity back on or determine a shift of preference of the RBD towards other glycans that can still be recognised within the N370 cleft.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential future mutations

claim: Earlier work shows SARS-CoV-2 S-based protein vaccines with increased efficacy due to the removal of N-glycans.
source: Indeed, earlier work shows SARS-CoV-2 S-based protein vaccines with increased efficacy due to the removal of N-glycans (Huang et al., 2022)
evidence: Supported by citation to Huang et al., 2022

claim: RBD-based vaccines are in use and under development that may be designed with and without N-glycans.
source: Indeed, earlier work shows SARS-CoV-2 S-based protein vaccines with increased efficacy due to the removal of N-glycans (Huang et al., 2022), and of RBD-based vaccines in use and under development (Cohen et al., 2022; Más-Bermejo et al., 2022; Valdes-Balbin et al., 2021) that may be designed with and without N-glycans.
evidence: Supported by citations to Cohen et al., 2022, Más-Bermejo et al., 2022, and Valdes-Balbin et al., 2021

claim: Taking into consideration the effects of N-glycosylation on protein structural stability and dynamics in the context of specific protein sequences may be key to understanding epistatic interactions among RBD residues.
source: Further to this, our results show that taking into consideration the effects on N-glycosylation on protein structural stability and dynamics in the context of specific protein sequences, may be key to understanding epistatic interactions among RBD residues (Rochman et al., 2022; Witte et al., 2023), which would be otherwise difficult, where not impossible, to decipher.
evidence: Supported by citations to Rochman et al., 2022 and Witte et al., 2023, and involves inference about the importance of glycosylation in understanding epistasis

claim: All simulations were performed using additive, all-atom force fields, namely the AMBER 14 SB parameter set to represent protein atoms and counterions, GLYCAM06j-1 to represent glycans, and TIP3P for water molecules.
source: All simulations were performed using additive, all-atom force fields, namely the AMBER 14 SB parameter set (Maier et al., 2015) to represent protein atoms and counterions (200 mM of NaCl), GLYCAM06j-1 (Kirschner et al., 2008) to represent glycans, and TIP3P for water molecules (Jorgensen et al., 1983).
evidence: This describes the computational methods used, supported by citations

claim: All production trajectories from conventional MD simulations were run for a minimum of 2 μs to ensure convergence.
source: All production trajectories from conventional (deterministic) MD simulations were run for a minimum of 2 μs to ensure convergence.
evidence: This describes the computational methods used

claim: All Gaussian accelerated MD (GaMD) production trajectories were run for 2 μs.
source: All Gaussian accelerated MD (GaMD) (Miao et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2021) production trajectories were run for 2 μs.
evidence: This describes the computational methods used, supported by citations

claim: The glycans at N331 and N343 were rebuilt as FA2G2 based on glycoproteomics data.
source: The glycans at N331 and N343 were rebuilt as FA2G2 (GlyTouCan-ID G00998NI) based on glycoproteomics data (Newby et al., 2023; Watanabe et al., 2020a) with 3D structures from our GlycoShape database (Ives et al., 2023) (https://glycoshape.org).
evidence: Supported by citations to glycoproteomics data and the GlycoShape database

claim: Over 45 μs of cumulative sampling from conventional and enhanced molecular dynamics simulations was performed.
source: In this work, we show through over 45 μs of cumulative sampling from conventional and enhanced molecular dynamics (MD) simulations
evidence: This describes the total computational sampling performed
